record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How can federated-learning implementations of differential privacy be audited for correctness, including black-box testing methods for systems whose organizations do not open-source their code?

evidence.quote: What techniques can be used for testing FL-implementations for correctness?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote a randomized mechanism implemented as part of a federated learning system that claims to satisfy $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy: for all neighboring data sets $D, D'$ (differing in one client's record) and all measurable output sets $S$,
$$\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D')\in S]+\delta.$$
Suppose the implementation of $\mathcal{M}$ is operated by an organization that does not release its source code, so the auditor only has black-box query access: the auditor may choose inputs (subject to realistic constraints on participation as a federated client) and observe the (possibly aggregated) outputs of $\mathcal{M}$, but cannot inspect internal state, randomness, or code.

Develop a methodology for auditing such a federated-learning implementation of differential privacy for correctness. Concretely:

1. Define a black-box auditing procedure $A$ that, given query access to $\mathcal{M}$ and a claimed privacy budget $(\varepsilon,\delta)$, outputs either "accept" or "reject" together with a statistical guarantee (e.g., a lower bound $\hat\varepsilon$ on the true privacy parameter with controlled Type I error).
2. Provide testing techniques applicable when the auditor cannot open-source-inspect the system, including the design of adversarial neighboring inputs (canaries), choice of test statistics, and methods that remain valid under the federated setting (multiple clients, secure aggregation, server-side noise).
3. Establish sample-complexity bounds and soundness/completeness guarantees showing that, under stated assumptions on the access model, common implementation bugs that violate $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP are detected with high probability.
artifact.status_search_result: Active research has produced multiple black-box and gray-box auditing methods for differentially private mechanisms (e.g., tight black-box auditing of DP-SGD, f-DP-based black-box estimation, sequential anytime-valid tests, and gray-box library audits). These provide partial answers — particularly for DP-SGD and standalone DP libraries — but a fully general, sample-efficient black-box auditing methodology tailored to closed-source federated learning systems with secure aggregation remains an active and only partially resolved problem.

status_evidence.title: Nearly Tight Black-Box Auditing of Differentially Private Machine Learning
status_evidence.snippet: presents an auditing procedure for the DP-SGD algorithm in the black-box threat model that is substantially tighter than prior work
status_evidence.claim: Black-box auditing of DP-SGD has been substantially advanced, indicating partial progress.

status_evidence.title: Auditing Differential Privacy in the Black-Box Setting
status_evidence.snippet: novel theoretical framework for auditing differential privacy in a black-box setting, leveraging f-differential privacy with controlled Type I/II errors
status_evidence.claim: General black-box auditing frameworks have been proposed but remain under active development.

status_evidence.title: Privacy in Theory, Bugs in Practice: Grey-Box Auditing of Differential Privacy Libraries
status_evidence.snippet: bugs that lead to DP violations have been found in several DP-SGD implementations ... gray-box auditing paradigm that assumes access to the underlying implementation
status_evidence.claim: Implementation bugs are still being uncovered; gray-box (not pure black-box) access is often needed.

status_evidence.title: Sequentially Auditing Differential Privacy
status_evidence.snippet: practical sequential test for auditing differential privacy guarantees of black-box mechanisms ... anytime-valid inference
status_evidence.claim: New sequential black-box auditing tests continue to appear, showing the area is still developing.
